title_original: Jeu de Paume : Stan Douglas : Parallax
excerpt_original: The Jeu de Paume presents the exhibition Parallax, the most significant solo exhibition devoted to Stan Douglas in France in more than 30 years. […] Cet article Jeu de Paume : Stan Douglas : Parallax est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: The Jeu de Paume presents the exhibition Parallax , the most significant solo exhibition devoted to Stan Douglas in France in more than 30 years. Born in Vancouver in 1960, the artist, a major figure on the international contemporary scene, presents some forty works – films, video installations, photographic series – spanning his entire career, from the late 1980s to today. After Paris, the exhibition will travel to the Museu d’Art Contemporani de Barcelona (MACBA) in 2027.

Photography holds a central place in Stan Douglas’s work. In series such as Crowds and Riots (2008), Midcentury Studio (2010–2011), Nocturnes (2014–2015), DCTs (2016–2017) or 2011 ≠ 1848 (2017–2021), the artist creates impossible images: portraits of vanished places, unique moments that cannot be reproduced, or historical scenes erased from the official archives and recreated with precision. His images, then, do not merely document the archive: they intervene in it, destabilize it and expose its silences.

Stan Douglas lives and works in Vancouver. Since the beginning of his career, he has developed a practice that combines the media of film and photography, and he is interested in the processes at work in the creation of reality, treating perception as a subject in its own right. In his installations, Douglas continues his reflections on the role of technology in the creation of images and on the way those images shape collective memory. All of his work, although rooted in a specific historical and cultural context, resonates far beyond it and finds a universal echo.

The exhibition’s title, “Parallax,” refers to the apparent displacement of an object depending on the viewer’s position. This optical phenomenon indeed shows that every gaze is oriented and contingent, arising from a partial perspective. In this sense, Douglas challenges linear and deterministic views of history in order to show that narratives are in perpetual construction and interruption. No image is neutral; no narrative can be considered complete.
Parallax offers an overview of Stan Douglas’s work, highlighting the relationship between the works and the historical moments they evoke, as well as how that relationship has evolved over time.

The exhibition takes stock of the artist’s varied contributions to the analysis of cinema as a medium, from Overture (1986), in which, in one of his first accomplished experiments in editing, he links railway technology, involuntary memory and the conventions of early cinema, to later installations such as Der Sandmann (1995), Suspiria (2003) or The Secret Agent (2015), in which he explores different registers and media.

Music is another common thread in his work. In his films and video installations, he uses music – not as illustration, but as a conceptual structure – to address questions of race, class and social inequality.

In Hors-champs (1992), a collective improvisation session by American musicians in a French studio is transformed into a reflection on diaspora and creativity. In Luanda-Kinshasa (2013), he reconstructs a fictional 1970s recording session in order to analyze the transatlantic collaborations behind new musical styles.

ISDN (2022), for its part, stages an imaginary dialogue between rappers from London and rappers from Cairo at the time of the Arab Spring and the riots that shook the United Kingdom after the killing of Mark Duggan by police officers. The many permutations this installation presents rule out any definitive answer.

The logic of permutation and recombination, based on a principle of repetition constantly renewed through variation, is one of Stan Douglas’s most distinctive formal devices. His narrative installations, such as Inconsolable Memories (2005) or The Secret Agent (2015), are governed by patterns that recombine fragments of history until every possibility has been exhausted. The absence of resolution does not signal a failing of the narrative; on the contrary, it is the condition of a future in which everything remains open, in which things could – and still can – happen differently.

For the first time in France, the exhibition presents one of Stan Douglas’s most recent works, Birth of a Nation (2025), a video installation that on its own sums up these lines of force with singular intensity.

By recomposing D.W. Griffith’s racist film of 1915, Douglas opens a breach in the victors’ narrative in order to give a voice back to those who were excluded or erased from it. Once again, it is history that could have been written differently, and a gaze cast from another place, that reveals what a single perspective will never be able to see.
Curators: Gloria Moure and Marta Ponsa for the Jeu de Paume version. Exhibition design: Cécile Degos
An exhibition co-produced with the Museu d’Art Contemporani de Barcelona (MACBA)
